newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu said to eye "unity" government.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu said to eye "unity" government.

text.p: With a crumbling peace process and raging West Bank violence, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may be looking to form a new "national unity" government that would bring in the main opposition Labour party.
Israeli officials are denying it but some analysts think it's inevitable.

"I would say that Netanyahu has more or less made up his mind that the only way to save the peace process and his standing at home and internationally is to form a national unity government," said political analyst Leslie Susser.

Israeli airwaves were abuzz with reports of backroom meetings between Likud party leader Netanyahu and Labour's Shimon Peres who has made no secret of his desire to join a government he says must be committed to peace.

"The prime minister has not decided to form a national unity government and any talk about its makeup, size and other details is journalistic speculation," Netanyahu's office said on Wednesday after the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth printed what it said was a lineup of Netanyahu's new cabinet.

The right-wing Netanyahu ousted Peres last May on election pledges that have proven difficult to square -- to build more homes for Jews in the West Bank while making peace with Yasser Arafat, to force the Palestinian leader to crack down on Islamic militants while halting concessions to the PLO.
Netanyahu opposed Israel's landmark 1993 accord with the PLO which Peres, a Nobel peace laureate, helped to engineer.

Netanyahu's religious and ultra-nationalist coalition partners accused him this month of ceding too much when he offered to hand over another nine percent of the West Bank to Palestinian self-rule but Arafat said it was precious little.

"A unity government would marginalise the right wing of the Likud, and the right-wing parties. That would allow Netanyahu to go ahead and make concessions to Arafat without having to compensate the right -- something he cannot do now," said political scientist Gerald Steinberg.

Netanyahu sent bulldozers last week to break ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in a gesture to his rightist coalition partners after handing over parts of the West Bank city of Hebron to the Palestinian Authority.
Palestinians responded with protests, and Islamic militants with a suicide bombing.
Peres called unity government rumours "baseless" but Yedioth Ahronoth's report gave Labour six seats in Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet including the important defence and finance portfolios.
It was enough to undermine Likud Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai's feeling of job security.
"The prime minster called this morning and told me to discard the newspapers because there's no truth in them," Mordechai told reporters.
"I'm sure that the position of defence minister is reserved for Likud and within the Likud it is reserved for the man currently serving as defence minister," he said.

Peres has said a unity government is the only way to save peace moves with the Palestinians and other Arab partners but he has formally postponed the issue until a criminal investigation against members of Netanyahu's cabinet is cleared up.

Police said on Wednesday it would take another 10 days to decide if cabinet members would be charged in the "Bar-On affair" involving the ill-fated appointment of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.
Netanyahu and his Justice Minister Tsahi Hanegbi have been questioned under police caution during the investigation.
"The main thing that's holding up a national unity government is the Bar-On scandal. Labour won't commit itself to a partnership with a prime minister who may not come out unscathed," Susser said.
